title: Global Food Prices Set to Surge as Iran War and El Niño Squeeze Supply Chains
excerpt: The FAO's chief economist warns that commodity prices will start climbing by year-end, with a full-blown food price spike likely in 2027 as the Strait of Hormuz closure drives up energy and fertilizer costs.
body:
• FAO chief economist Maximo Torero told Reuters he expects food commodity prices to start rising by year-end, with a sharper increase in 2027
  • The Strait of Hormuz closure has driven up oil and natural gas prices, raising costs for fertilizer, transportation, packaging, and processing across global agriculture
  • Wheat prices are already 7.8% higher year-on-year, with U.S. Hard Red Winter wheat up 28% since May 2025 due to poor crop conditions and higher input costs
  • The FAO Food Price Index has risen for two consecutive months to its highest level since December, and the WFP warns 45 million more people could face acute hunger if the conflict persists

The world is heading for another bout of food inflation as the Iran war, the Ukraine conflict, and El Niño converge to push up costs and threaten crop yields, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization's chief economist has warned.

"I expect that commodity prices will start to increase more now ... and food prices will start increasing by the end of the year, and next year for sure they will increase more," Maximo Torero told Reuters in an interview published Wednesday. He noted that the transmission lag from commodity to consumer food prices runs three to six months.

The Hormuz Factor

The Strait of Hormuz — which carried roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments before the U.S.-Iran war began — has been largely closed since hostilities escalated. The disruption has sent shockwaves through agricultural supply chains in ways that go well beyond fuel.

"The Strait of Hormuz is a problem that affects all the inputs of agricultural commodities, agricultural systems," Torero said. "Brent oil, because it's used for pumping, packaging, processing, and transportation. And natural gas because it's used for fertilizers."

Meanwhile, Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure have further curtailed diesel and natural gas exports, both critical inputs in food production. Since commodity prices are global, the pain spreads worldwide even if richer countries have more cash to cushion their farmers.

Where Prices Stand Now

The FAO Food Price Index has risen for two consecutive months to its highest level since December, standing 1% above its year-ago mark. The cereal price index jumped 2.6% in May from April, driven by higher prices across all major grains.

Wheat prices tell the starkest story. International wheat rose 3.4% month-on-month in May and 7.8% year-on-year, reflecting poor harvests in the United States, where winter wheat conditions are among the worst in decades. U.S. Hard Red Winter wheat prices were 28% higher in May 2026 than a year earlier. Maize edged up 1.9% on tighter availability in Brazil and the U.S., while rice rose 2.7% on weather concerns and higher energy costs.

"Those choices will hit future yields and shape our food supply and commodity prices for the rest of this year and all of the next."

— Maximo Torero, FAO Chief Economist, on farmers reducing inputs due to high costs

India and the Diaspora

India is particularly exposed. The country imports large volumes of edible oils and fertilizers, both of which have been affected by the Hormuz disruption. Rising global wheat and rice prices could pressure domestic food inflation, which the Reserve Bank of India has been working to contain. For the Indian diaspora, higher food costs in both India and host countries mean a double squeeze — remittances buy less, and grocery bills at home climb.

The World Food Programme estimates that 318 million people already face crisis-level hunger, and its March analysis warned that 45 million more could be pushed into acute food insecurity if the Middle East conflict persists.

What's Next

The calm in food markets so far this year has been deceptive, buffered by relatively good prior harvests and ample cereal stocks. But if input costs remain elevated beyond 40 days, the FAO warns that farmers will face hard choices — farming with fewer inputs, planting less, or switching to less fertilizer-intensive crops. Those decisions, made now, will determine harvests in autumn 2026 and shape prices well into 2027.
